illustrations.title: Turn “safe” into a checkable requirement
illustrations.caption: Create a task successfully, restart the process, and check that the task remains. This requirement concerns a process restart with committed storage intact.

illustrations.title: Choose, record, and review a design
illustrations.caption: Write down the requirements, compare choices, and record the decision. Later, use measurements and changed requirements to decide whether the design still fits.
illustrations.why: Keep the reasons for a decision alongside the decision itself.

illustrations.title: Check requirements before scoring preferences
illustrations.caption: Memory-only storage loses tasks after restart, so we reject it for this application. We compare preference scores only for choices that meet the required behaviour.
illustrations.why: An easy-to-run choice is useful only if it meets the requirements.

illustrations.title: Availability and durability answer different questions
illustrations.caption: A service may reply to requests yet lose tasks after restart. Another may keep every committed task but stop accepting requests while it recovers.
illustrations.why: Check both whether requests succeed and whether saved data survives the stated failure.

illustrations.title: One program, two processes, three threads
illustrations.caption: The same upload program starts two processes. Threads 1 and 2 can reach document A inside process A; thread 3 belongs to process B and reaches its separate document B.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: What memory is shared?
illustrations.caption: Each thread has its own active call frames. Both threads hold references to the same upload buffer on the heap. Exact storage layout depends on the language and runtime.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: A single core schedules several threads
illustrations.caption: Time advances through A, B, then A again on one core. A waits for storage while B executes. Becoming runnable after I/O does not guarantee that A runs immediately.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Computing time versus waiting time
illustrations.caption: Each bar divides one file’s assumed elapsed time into computing and waiting. The two bars show proportions, not equal durations or measured throughput.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Synchronous and asynchronous execution
illustrations.caption: Time runs down each pair of participants. The synchronous caller waits for the reply; the asynchronous arrangement allows other ready work before completion. Neither picture implies an extra CPU core.

illustrations.title: Blocking vs nonblocking I/O
illustrations.caption: With no bytes ready, a blocking call keeps its thread waiting. A nonblocking call returns “not ready”; a readiness notification tells the program when to try again. Neither return nor readiness means the whole file has arrived.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Concurrency is not parallelism
illustrations.caption: On one core, A and B alternate. On two cores, their execution overlaps. The first is concurrent progress; the second also demonstrates parallel execution.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Follow a task through the event loop
illustrations.caption: A submits I/O and suspends. The loop runs other ready work, then makes A ready after completion. A long callback prevents this one thread from attending to other ready tasks.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: The bounded worker pool
illustrations.caption: J1 and J2 occupy both workers; J3–J5 occupy all three waiting slots. J6 therefore requires an overload response. A worker limit alone does not bound the waiting queue.

illustrations.title: Shared value or explicit message
illustrations.caption: On the left, both threads can change one shared counter. On the right, workers send increment messages to a counter owner, which handles them one at a time. Delivery and retry rules remain separate decisions.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: How one increment gets lost
illustrations.caption: Time runs down. Both threads read 0 before either stores an increment. They each compute 1 and eventually store 1, so one of the two intended increments is lost.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Which coordination tool solves which problem?
illustrations.caption: A mutex limits ownership to one participant; a two-permit semaphore admits two. An atomic update protects its defined operation. A condition-variable waiter must recheck its predicate using the associated synchronization protocol.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: A deadlock has a circular wait
illustrations.caption: Green arrows run from each held lock to its owner. Red dashed arrows run from each waiting thread to the lock it needs. X is the file lock; Y is the counter lock. Follow A → Y → B → X → A: both threads retain the first lock while waiting for the second.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Visibility needs a synchronization edge
illustrations.caption: The writer initializes the result and releases a mutex. The reader acquires that same mutex and reads the result. Under the language’s mutex rules, the write happens before the protected read; elapsed time alone supplies no such guarantee.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Immutable sharing and guarded mutation
illustrations.caption: The immutable result can be read after safe publication without protecting further writes to that result. The mutable counter needs a protocol for every access. An immutable reference alone does not freeze its target object.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: When arrivals exceed service capacity
illustrations.caption: With a constant excess of 50 jobs per second and an initially empty queue, waiting work reaches 100 after two seconds in this illustrative fluid model. At capacity, reject or defer input; a bounded queue does not increase completion rate.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

illustrations.title: Cancellation propagates through a task family
illustrations.caption: Cancellation reaches children in the parent’s task scope. The scope waits for their cleanup under the runtime’s rules. An upload may already have caused an external effect, so stopping its task is not a business rollback.
illustrations.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: The application and storage work together
figures.caption: The application needs storage to keep a task after restart. We include both inside the boundary when discussing that requirement.
figures.why: Include the parts needed to explain the behaviour you are studying.

figures.title: Creating a task changes the stored state
figures.caption: Before creation, the collection is empty. After create(7, “Read”), it contains task 7, marked incomplete. The function returns the task details.
figures.why: Read the state before and after the operation to see exactly what changed.

figures.title: Save before reporting success
figures.caption: Memory-only tasks disappear after restart. In the revised version, the application commits the task before reporting success. The task remains after a process restart if committed storage is intact.
figures.why: Compare the two versions by restarting the process.

figures.title: Two levels of detail in one design
figures.caption: The high-level view shows the application and database. The low-level view shows the service, repository interface, and rules inside the application.
figures.why: Check that both views agree about saving a task before reporting success.

figures.title: Shared storage details make changes spread
figures.caption: Several parts read or change the same task data directly. A change to a field or rule may therefore require edits in several places.
figures.why: Follow the arrows to find which parts know about the shared data.

figures.title: Separate responsibilities inside one process
figures.caption: The adapter reads input, the service checks task rules, and the repository saves and reads tasks. These parts all run inside one application process.
figures.why: Each kind of work has a clear place in the code.

figures.title: The service uses a repository contract
figures.caption: The service uses the repository interface. The SQLite adapter implements that interface. Startup code creates the adapter and passes it to the service; during execution, the service calls it.
figures.why: The dashed arrows show code dependencies. These objects can run in the same process.

figures.title: Each layer works at a different level of detail
figures.caption: The user asks to remember a task. The application applies task rules and requests a storage write. Storage uses files and the underlying device to carry out the write.
figures.why: Follow one request through the layers to connect the user’s action to the work below it.

figures.title: Turn “safe” into a checkable requirement
figures.caption: Create a task successfully, restart the process, and check that the task remains. This requirement concerns a process restart with committed storage intact.
figures.why: A specific requirement tells us which test to run.

figures.title: Choose, record, and review a design
figures.caption: Write down the requirements, compare choices, and record the decision. Later, use measurements and changed requirements to decide whether the design still fits.
figures.why: Keep the reasons for a decision alongside the decision itself.

figures.title: Check requirements before scoring preferences
figures.caption: Memory-only storage loses tasks after restart, so we reject it for this application. We compare preference scores only for choices that meet the required behaviour.
figures.why: An easy-to-run choice is useful only if it meets the requirements.

figures.title: Availability and durability answer different questions
figures.caption: A service may reply to requests yet lose tasks after restart. Another may keep every committed task but stop accepting requests while it recovers.
figures.why: Check both whether requests succeed and whether saved data survives the stated failure.

figures.title: C4: zoom from the system into its code
figures.caption: Each step shows more internal detail. The dashed arrows mean “zoom in.” In C4, a container is an application or data store; it need not be a Docker container.
figures.why: Select the level that helps your reader answer a particular question.

figures.title: The application and database share one machine
figures.caption: The browser sends requests to an application on one machine. The database file is on that same machine. If the machine fails, the application and access to the file are both affected.
figures.why: Show physical placement when asking what can fail together.

figures.title: The task is saved, but the reply is lost
figures.caption: Task 7 is committed before its reply is lost. The client cannot tell what happened. A fresh create request may add task 8 unless the application recognises it as a retry.
figures.why: Trace the events in order to see why the client can be unsure even when a task exists.

figures.title: Each design change answers a new need

figures.title: Blocking vs nonblocking I/O

figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Concurrency is not parallelism
figures.caption: On one core, A and B alternate. On two cores, their execution overlaps. The first is concurrent progress; the second also demonstrates parallel execution.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Follow a task through the event loop
figures.caption: A submits I/O and suspends. The loop runs other ready work, then makes A ready after completion. A long callback prevents this one thread from attending to other ready tasks.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: The bounded worker pool
figures.caption: J1 and J2 occupy both workers; J3–J5 occupy all three waiting slots. J6 therefore requires an overload response. A worker limit alone does not bound the waiting queue.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Shared value or explicit message
figures.caption: On the left, both threads can change one shared counter. On the right, workers send increment messages to a counter owner, which handles them one at a time. Delivery and retry rules remain separate decisions.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: How one increment gets lost
figures.caption: Time runs down. Both threads read 0 before either stores an increment. They each compute 1 and eventually store 1, so one of the two intended increments is lost.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Which coordination tool solves which problem?
figures.caption: A mutex limits ownership to one participant; a two-permit semaphore admits two. An atomic update protects its defined operation. A condition-variable waiter must recheck its predicate using the associated synchronization protocol.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: A deadlock has a circular wait
figures.caption: Green arrows run from each held lock to its owner. Red dashed arrows run from each waiting thread to the lock it needs. X is the file lock; Y is the counter lock. Follow A → Y → B → X → A: both threads retain the first lock while waiting for the second.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Visibility needs a synchronization edge
figures.caption: The writer initializes the result and releases a mutex. The reader acquires that same mutex and reads the result. Under the language’s mutex rules, the write happens before the protected read; elapsed time alone supplies no such guarantee.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Immutable sharing and guarded mutation
figures.caption: The immutable result can be read after safe publication without protecting further writes to that result. The mutable counter needs a protocol for every access. An immutable reference alone does not freeze its target object.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: When arrivals exceed service capacity
figures.caption: With a constant excess of 50 jobs per second and an initially empty queue, waiting work reaches 100 after two seconds in this illustrative fluid model. At capacity, reject or defer input; a bounded queue does not increase completion rate.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.

figures.title: Cancellation propagates through a task family
figures.caption: Cancellation reaches children in the parent’s task scope. The scope waits for their cleanup under the runtime’s rules. An upload may already have caused an external effect, so stopping its task is not a business rollback.
figures.why: Trace the objects, states and ordering described in the caption.
